q: The light-initiated chlorination of methane is a radical chain reaction. Which step is a termination step?
h: Count the radicals on each side of the arrow. Which kind of step lowers the number of radicals?
w: A termination step combines two radicals into a nonradical product, so the number of radicals drops by two and the chain stops. CH3• + Cl• → CH3Cl has two radicals on the left and none on the right. Homolysis of Cl2 makes radicals (initiation), and the two steps that consume one radical and make another are propagation steps.
x: Homolysis of Cl<sub>2</sub> by light creates two radicals from a nonradical; that is initiation.
One radical in, one radical out: this is the second propagation step, which regenerates the Cl• chain carrier.
One radical in, one radical out: this is the first propagation step (H abstraction).

q: Which radical is the most stable?
h: Two effects stabilize a carbon radical: delocalization into a π system and the number of alkyl groups on the radical carbon.
w: Radicals are stabilized by resonance (allylic, benzylic) and by alkyl substitution (hyperconjugation). The 2-phenyl-2-propyl radical, C6H5–C•(CH3)2, is both benzylic (the odd electron is delocalized into the ring) and tertiary, so it has both effects. Benzyl is benzylic but only primary; tert-butyl is tertiary but has no resonance; the vinylic radical is the least stable of the four.
x: Benzyl is resonance-stabilized, but it is primary; adding two methyl groups to the same benzylic carbon stabilizes it further.
tert-Butyl is tertiary but not delocalized; a benzylic radical gains much more from resonance than from hyperconjugation alone.
The odd electron of a vinylic radical sits in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital in the plane of the π bond, so it is not delocalized; vinylic radicals are very unstable.

q:
Rank these radicals from least stable to most stable.
I. CH2=CH•
II. CH3CH2CH2•
III. (CH3)3C•
IV. CH2=CH–CH•–CH3
h: Place the vinylic radical first, then compare a tertiary alkyl radical with a secondary allylic one.
w: Vinylic radicals (I) are the least stable: the odd electron is in an sp2 orbital and cannot be delocalized. Among alkyl radicals, 3° (III) is more stable than 1° (II). The secondary allylic radical IV is delocalized over two carbons, and allylic resonance outweighs one extra alkyl group, so IV is the most stable (a 2° allylic C–H bond is roughly 50 kJ/mol weaker than a 3° C–H). Order: I < II < III < IV.
x: A primary alkyl radical is still more stable than a vinylic radical, whose odd electron sits in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital with no hyperconjugative or resonance help.
This puts the 3° alkyl radical above the allylic radical; resonance delocalization in IV stabilizes more than the extra alkyl group in III.
The vinylic radical is the least stable, not the most; sp<sup>2</sup> character does not stabilize a radical the way it stabilizes a carbanion.

q: Which hydrogen is abstracted most easily by a bromine atom? (The labels mark the carbons; consider an H on each labeled carbon.)
h: The easiest H to remove is the one whose C–H bond is weakest, which is the one that leaves the most stable radical.
w: Removing an H on carbon b gives a radical next to the C=C, an allylic radical delocalized onto the terminal CH2. Allylic C–H bonds (roughly 350–370 kJ/mol) are weaker than a 3° C–H (about 400 kJ/mol), so the H on carbon b goes first. Carbon c is tertiary but not allylic; a is vinylic (strong sp2 C–H); d is a primary C–H.
x: Carbon c gives a 3° alkyl radical, but an allylic radical is more stable than a 3° radical because the odd electron is delocalized.
Carbon a is a vinylic C–H: an sp2 C–H is strong, and the vinylic radical cannot be delocalized.
Carbon d is a methyl group; a primary C–H gives the least stable alkyl radical.

q: 2-Methylbutane is treated with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light at 25 °C. Using relative rates per H of 1° : 2° : 3° = 1 : 3.8 : 5, what percentage of the monochlorinated product is 2-chloro-2-methylbutane?
h: For each kind of H, multiply the number of hydrogens by the rate per H, then divide the 3° share by the total.
w: Count H: two equivalent CH3 on C2 (6 H, 1°), C2–H (1 H, 3°), C3 CH2 (2 H, 2°), C4 CH3 (3 H, 1°). Relative amounts: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane 6 × 1 = 6; 2-chloro-2-methylbutane 1 × 5 = 5; 2-chloro-3-methylbutane 2 × 3.8 = 7.6; 1-chloro-3-methylbutane 3 × 1 = 3. Total 21.6. Tertiary chloride = 5/21.6 = 23%. Chlorination is fast and unselective, so the statistical factor (number of H) matters a lot.
x: 35% is the share of 2-chloro-3-methylbutane (7.6/21.6), the 2° product, not the 3° product.
46% comes from 5/(1 + 3.8 + 5 + 1), which uses rates but ignores how many H of each kind there are.
8.3% is 1/12, a purely statistical count that ignores that a 3° H reacts 5 times faster than a 1° H.

q: 3-Methylpentane is brominated with Br<sub>2</sub> and light. Using relative rates per H of 1° : 2° : 3° = 1 : 82 : 1600, what percentage of the monobromide is 3-bromo-3-methylpentane?
h: Classify all 14 hydrogens first (how many 1°, 2° and 3° H are there?), then weight each class by its rate.
w: 3-Methylpentane has 9 primary H (three CH3 groups), 4 secondary H (two CH2 groups) and 1 tertiary H. Weighted amounts: 1°: 9 × 1 = 9; 2°: 4 × 82 = 328; 3°: 1 × 1600 = 1600. Total = 1937. 3-Bromo-3-methylpentane = 1600/1937 = 83%. Bromination is far more selective than chlorination (compare about 17% for the same 3° product with Cl2), but the four 2° H still take a noticeable share.
x: 90% (1600/1773) counts only 2 secondary H; there are two CH<sub>2</sub> groups, so 4 secondary H.
95% (1600/1683) uses the rates per H without multiplying by the number of each kind of H.
17% is what the chlorination rates (1 : 3.8 : 5) give; the question uses the bromination rates.

q: Why is radical bromination of alkanes much more selective than radical chlorination?
c: H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, so its transition state is late and radical-like, and radical stability differences show up strongly in the activation energies.
H abstraction by Br• is exothermic, so its transition state is early and resembles the alkane, which makes the different C–H bonds react at very different rates.
Br• is more reactive than Cl•, so it reacts with the weakest C–H bond before it can reach the stronger ones.
The Br–Br bond is weaker than the Cl–Cl bond, so more Br• forms and the most stable radical is reached faster.
h: Use the Hammond postulate: is the H-abstraction step uphill or downhill for each halogen, and what does that say about where its transition state lies?
w: The selectivity-determining step is H abstraction. For Br• it is endothermic (H–Br is weaker than most C–H bonds), so by the Hammond postulate the transition state is late and looks like the alkyl radical; the 3° > 2° > 1° stability gap is largely felt in Ea. For Cl• the step is exothermic, the TS is early and alkane-like, and the rates differ little. Hence the endothermic, late-TS step for Br• makes bromination selective.
x: This reverses the energetics: H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, and an early, reactant-like TS would make a reaction less selective, not more.
Br• is less reactive than Cl•. The lower reactivity (higher E<sub>a</sub>) is the reason it can discriminate between C–H bonds.
The Br–Br bond strength affects initiation, not which C–H bond is broken; selectivity is set in the H-abstraction step.

q:
Use the bond dissociation energies in the table. What is ΔH for the first propagation step of the bromination of propane at C2?
Br• + CH3CH2CH3 → HBr + (CH3)2CH•
h: ΔH = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed). Which bond breaks and which forms in this one step?
w: One bond breaks, (CH3)2CH–H (413 kJ/mol), and one forms, H–Br (366 kJ/mol). ΔH = 413 − 366 = +47 kJ/mol. This endothermic step is why bromination is slow and selective. The second step, (CH3)2CH• + Br2, is 193 − 299 = −106 kJ/mol, so the chain is still downhill overall.
x: Sign error: subtract energy of bonds formed from bonds broken (413 − 366), not the reverse.
−18 kJ/mol is the same step for chlorination (413 − 431), using H–Cl instead of H–Br.
−59 kJ/mol is ΔH for the overall bromination (sum of both propagation steps), not the first step alone.

q: (S)-3-Methylhexane is treated with Br2 and light. Which describes the major product, 3-bromo-3-methylhexane?
c: A single enantiomer with the same spatial arrangement as the starting alkane
A single enantiomer with the inverted arrangement
Two diastereomers formed in unequal amounts
h: Which H is removed, and what is the shape of the radical carbon that forms?
w: Br• removes the 3° H, which is on the stereocenter itself. The resulting 3° radical is planar (or rapidly inverting), so the original configuration is lost, and Br2 delivers Br to either face equally. The product is racemic 3-bromo-3-methylhexane.
x: Retention would require the radical to stay pyramidal with a fixed shape; the stereocenter is destroyed when its H is removed.
Inversion is the SN2 outcome (backside attack). A radical halogenation has no backside attack; the planar radical reacts on both faces.
Diastereomers need a second stereocenter that survives the reaction. Here the only stereocenter is the carbon that becomes the radical.

q: (S)-2-Chlorobutane is chlorinated with Cl2 and light. Considering only the 2,3-dichlorobutane formed, which statement is correct?
c: It is a mixture of meso-2,3-dichlorobutane and (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane in unequal amounts.
It is a mixture of meso-2,3-dichlorobutane and (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane in exactly equal amounts.
It is a racemic mixture of (2R,3R)- and (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane.
It is only (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane, because C2 blocks one face of the radical completely.
h: C2 is not touched when the H on C3 is removed. Which configurations can the new stereocenter at C3 have, and how are the two products related?
w: Abstraction of an H from C3 leaves C2 unchanged (still S; its priorities Cl > CHClCH3 > CH3 > H keep the same order). Cl adds to either face of the planar C3 radical, giving C3 = R or S. (2S,3R) is the meso compound; (2S,3S) is chiral. The two faces of the radical are diastereotopic (C2 is a nearby stereocenter), so the transition states are diastereomeric and the products form in unequal amounts: meso + (2S,3S).
x: The two faces of the C3 radical are not mirror images because C2 is a stereocenter; diastereomeric transition states have different energies, so 50:50 is not expected.
C2 keeps its S configuration, so no (2R,3R) product can form from (S)-2-chlorobutane.
A neighboring stereocenter biases the two faces but does not block one completely; both diastereomers form.

h: With peroxide present, which species adds to the alkene first: H<sup>+</sup> or Br•?
w: Peroxides start a radical chain in which Br• adds to the less substituted carbon (CH2) to give the more stable 3° radical, which then takes H from HBr. Br ends up on the less substituted carbon: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, the anti-Markovnikov product.
x: tert-Butyl bromide is the Markovnikov product of the ionic (no peroxide) HBr addition via a 3° carbocation.
An anti-Markovnikov alcohol comes from hydroboration–oxidation; no oxygen is added here.
A vicinal dibromide comes from Br<sub>2</sub> addition, not from HBr.

q: In the radical chain addition of HBr (with ROOR) to 1-methylcyclohexene, what happens in the first propagation step?
c: Br• adds to carbon b, leaving a 3° radical on carbon a
Br• adds to carbon a, leaving a 2° radical on carbon b
H• adds to carbon b, leaving a 3° radical on carbon a
H+ adds to carbon b, leaving a 3° carbocation on carbon a
h: The chain carrier is made when RO• takes H from HBr. Which radical is that, and where must it add to leave the more stable radical?
w: Initiation: RO• + HBr → ROH + Br•. Propagation step 1: Br• adds to carbon b (the CH end), leaving the 3° radical on carbon a. Step 2: that radical takes H from HBr, giving 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane and a new Br•. The regiochemistry is set by radical stability, which is why Br ends up on the less substituted carbon.
x: Adding Br• to carbon a would leave the less stable 2° radical; the favored path gives the 3° radical.
H• is not a chain carrier; RO• abstracts H from HBr (forming the strong O–H bond), so Br• is what adds.
That is the ionic (Markovnikov) mechanism without peroxide; it gives 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.

q: 1-Methylcyclohexene is treated with HBr in the presence of a peroxide. Which best describes the product?
c: 1-Bromo-2-methylcyclohexane, as a mixture of cis and trans isomers (each racemic)
h: Decide the regiochemistry from the radical mechanism first, then count the new stereocenters and ask whether anything in the reaction is chiral.
w: Br• adds to the CH carbon to give the 3° radical, which then picks up H from HBr. The product, 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane, has two stereocenters (C1 and C2). H can be delivered to either face of the radical, so both cis and trans diastereomers form, and because all reagents are achiral each is racemic: a mixture of cis and trans 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane.
x: Br on the more substituted carbon is the Markovnikov product of the ionic mechanism; peroxide switches to the radical path.
Achiral starting materials and reagents cannot give a single enantiomer, and the radical intermediate does not enforce one relative stereochemistry.
Allylic substitution needs a low, steady Br<sub>2</sub> concentration (NBS); with HBr the radical chain adds across the C=C bond.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: NBS keeps the Br<sub>2</sub> concentration very low. Which C–H bond in cyclohexene is weakest?
w: NBS supplies Br2 at a very low concentration, so addition to the C=C is too slow and radical substitution wins. Br• removes an allylic H (the weakest C–H), the allylic radical takes Br from Br2, and the product is 3-bromocyclohexene. In cyclohexene both ends of the allylic radical give the same compound.
x: Vinylic C–H bonds are strong and the vinylic radical is not stabilized, so the H on the double bond is not removed.
The 1,2-dibromide forms when Br<sub>2</sub> is present at high concentration (Br<sub>2</sub> in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>), not with NBS.
Bromocyclohexane would need HBr addition; NBS substitutes an allylic H and keeps the C=C.

q: But-1-ene is treated with NBS and light. Which set of products forms?
h: Draw the allylic radical from C3 and its resonance form. Where can Br attach?
w: Br• removes a 2° allylic H at C3. The radical is delocalized: CH2=CH–CH•–CH3 ↔ •CH2–CH=CH–CH3. Br2 can trap either end. At C3 the product is 3-bromobut-1-ene (new stereocenter, racemic); at C1 the allylic shift gives 1-bromobut-2-ene, whose new C2=C3 bond can be E or Z. Answer: 3-bromobut-1-ene and (E/Z)-1-bromobut-2-ene.
x: This ignores the resonance form of the allylic radical; Br can also bond at C1, with the double bond shifting to C2=C3.
4-Bromobut-1-ene would need abstraction at the C4 methyl, which is not allylic and gives a less stable 1° radical.
Addition of Br<sub>2</sub> across the C=C is suppressed by the very low Br<sub>2</sub> concentration NBS provides.
